subject: 🧮 Anthropic Claude jumps Riemann Hypothesis from 41% to 67% in history
intro: AI is no longer just answering questions. It's doing the work. Claude failed to prove the Riemann Hypothesis (obviously) but stumbled onto the biggest single jump in 160 years of math history. OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Cyber found zero-days in Chrome before most humans even knew to look. Both unreleased, both already outperforming the field. The pattern is clear: the most interesting AI results are happening before the models ship.

news.headline: Anthropic's unreleased Claude model pushes Riemann hypothesis progress from 41.6% to 67.2%
news.body: Someone told Claude to take a real stab at one of math's hardest unsolved problems. Claude failed. But what it found on the way down is interesting. The Riemann Hypothesis is a 160-year-old math problem about where a special function hits zero. Think of it like a treasure map where all the X marks should land on one specific line. Nobody has proven they all do. The best humans could do was prove that at least 41.6% of those X marks land where expected. Claude just pushed that to 67.2% , the biggest single jump in history on this problem. It did this by treating the zeros as one unified space instead of analyzing them separately. The proof code and process logs are all public. The model is unreleased, but the agent architecture is yours to study today.
bullets: Used 60 AI subagents running in parallel inside Claude Code
Tried 650 failed ideas before finding the approach that worked
Ran 2,400 shell commands over a day and a half
Proof verified in Lean 4 and reviewed by two external math experts

news.headline: OpenAI ships GPT-5.6-Cyber, a model that found zero-days in Chrome's V8 engine
news.body: OpenAI just split its Daybreak cybersecurity program into two tiers, and the difference matters a lot depending on what you're building. Daybreak Blue is the starting point. You get GPT-5.6 Sol with security guardrails loosened just enough for defensive work. Think of it as the standard model, but it won't refuse you when you ask it to analyze malware or review vulnerable code. Daybreak Red is the serious tier. It unlocks GPT-5.6-Cyber , a model specifically trained to do the risky stuff: finding zero-day vulnerabilities (unknown security holes), building exploit chains, and validating attacks. It completed 95% of advanced security tasks in testing, versus just 1.5% for the regular GPT-5.6. Red access requires approval. You apply, get vetted, then get monitored. Not open to everyone yet.
bullets: Blue: vulnerability discovery, malware analysis, code review, incident response
Red: exploit development, zero-day research, security testing
Real proof: it found two unknown bugs in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine

news.headline: NVIDIA releases open 30B model that runs 4x faster than similar-sized models
news.body: NVIDIA just dropped Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , and the story here is speed without the usual tradeoff. Most AI agents waste compute. They use a massive, slow model for every single step, even boring ones like calling a tool or checking a result. Lightning fixes that. Here is the trick: it has 30B total parameters but only activates 3B at a time . Think of it like a team of specialists where only the right people show up for each task, instead of the whole company attending every meeting. That is the MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) design. The numbers back it up: You can fine-tune it on your own data using NVIDIA NeMo for domains like cybersecurity, coding, or legal work. Weights are open on Hugging Face, deployable via vLLM or SGLang today.
bullets: 86% accuracy on PinchBench, completing 10,000 tasks 35% faster than Qwen3 35B
1M token context window for long agent sessions
Runs on a single H100 or DGX Spark
